claims.text: Rhenium atoms in tungsten reduce the Peierls barrier for screw-dislocation motion.
Rhenium lowers the activation energy for kink-pair nucleation in tungsten.
The reduced kink-pair nucleation barrier increases dislocation mobility at elevated temperatures.
Increased dislocation mobility enhances plastic strain and fracture toughness.
The controlled intervention is addition of 3 at% Re to pure W under otherwise identical thermomechanical processing.
Reduced Peierls stress, quantified through the activation energy for kink-pair formation, is the proposed structural mediator.
Local electronic interactions between Re atoms and the W lattice lower lattice friction on screw dislocations.
Lower lattice friction enables sustained high-temperature dislocation glide.
Sustained high-temperature dislocation glide promotes crack-tip blunting.
At 800 °C, W–3Re is predicted to have at least 50% higher uniform elongation than pure W.
At 800 °C, W–3Re is predicted to have at least 20% higher fracture toughness than pure W.
Pure W has approximately 2% uniform elongation at 800 °C under the proposed test conditions.
Pure W has a fracture toughness of approximately 10 MPa·√m at 800 °C under the proposed test conditions.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for approximately 1–5 at% Re and temperatures from 700 °C to 1200 °C.
Outside the stated composition and temperature ranges, other deformation or fracture mechanisms may dominate.
The magnitude of improvement may vary by ±20% because of grain-size, texture, and residual-stress differences.
A decrease of less than 5% in activation energy, combined with no property improvement beyond the specified experimental uncertainties, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Pure W and W–3Re cannot literally be specimens drawn from the same compositionally homogeneous ingot. Separate ingots or compositionally distinct regions would be required, weakening the stated control unless processing and microstructure are independently matched.
